title: Cold Exposure, Immersion & Hypothermia
summary: Understand heat production and conservation in the cold and the injuries cold causes.

lessons.title: Shivering and Brown Fat Non-Shivering Thermogenesis

levels.kid:
Your body is like a cozy house with a furnace inside. It likes to stay at about 37 degrees Celsius. When you get cold, your brain turns up the heat in two ways.

First, you **shiver**. Your muscles shake very fast. Shaking muscles burn fuel, and burning fuel makes heat, just like rubbing your hands together makes them warm.

Second, you have a special kind of fat called **brown fat**. Most fat just stores energy, like a pantry. Brown fat is different. It burns energy on purpose just to make heat, like a tiny heater. Babies have lots of it around their necks and shoulders, because they can't shiver well yet.

Together, shivering and brown fat help keep you warm.
levels.hs:
Humans are **endotherms**: we make our own heat to keep core temperature near 37 °C. When skin and core temperature sensors detect cold, a brain region called the **hypothalamus** (specifically the preoptic area) triggers heat production, or **thermogenesis**.

There are two main types:
- **Shivering thermogenesis**: rapid, involuntary contractions of skeletal muscles. Because the muscles do no useful outside work, almost all the energy from breaking down ATP becomes heat. Intense shivering can raise heat production to about 4-5 times resting levels, but it is tiring and makes fine movements clumsy.
- **Non-shivering thermogenesis**: heat made without muscle movement, mainly by **brown adipose tissue (BAT)**. Brown fat cells are packed with **mitochondria**, which contain iron and give the tissue its brown colour.

Normally mitochondria use the energy in food to make ATP. In brown fat, a protein called **UCP1 (uncoupling protein 1)** lets protons leak back across the mitochondrial membrane, so the energy is released as heat instead of being stored in ATP. Think of a hydroelectric dam where water bypasses the turbines.

A real example: **newborns** rely heavily on brown fat between their shoulder blades because they shiver poorly. PET scans show that adults also keep active brown fat, mostly around the neck, collarbones and spine.
levels.college:
**Sensing and control.** Cutaneous cold receptors (largely **TRPM8**-expressing afferents) relay through the spinal dorsal horn to the lateral parabrachial nucleus, then to the **median preoptic area** of the hypothalamus. Cold inhibits warm-sensitive preoptic neurons and so disinhibits sympathetic and somatic output pathways. Key relays are the dorsomedial hypothalamus and the **rostral raphe pallidus** in the medulla, which drives both BAT sympathetic nerves and shivering motor neurons.

**Shivering.**
- Involuntary, rhythmic, asynchronous contractions of antagonist muscles, so little net movement occurs
- Usually begins in trunk and proximal muscles
- Peak heat production around 4-5x resting metabolic rate
- Low-intensity shivering relies largely on fat oxidation and type I fibres; high-intensity bursts recruit type II fibres and lean on muscle glycogen
- Limited by fuel depletion, fatigue and hypoglycaemia

**Brown adipose tissue.**
- Multilocular lipid droplets, dense mitochondria, rich capillary and sympathetic supply
- Norepinephrine acts on **β3-adrenergic receptors** (in humans β2 may dominate), raising cAMP and activating PKA
- PKA drives lipolysis, and the released fatty acids both fuel oxidation and directly activate **UCP1**
- UCP1 in the inner mitochondrial membrane dissipates the proton gradient, uncoupling respiration from ATP synthesis, so substrate energy is released as heat
- Purine nucleotides (ATP, ADP, GDP) tonically inhibit UCP1

**Thyroid hormone** works with sympathetic input: BAT expresses **type 2 deiodinase (DIO2)**, which converts T4 to active T3 locally and boosts UCP1 expression.

**Beige (brite) adipocytes** are UCP1-positive cells that appear within white fat after cold exposure or β-adrenergic stimulation. This process is called browning.

In adults, non-shivering thermogenesis contributes modestly compared with shivering, but repeated cold exposure increases BAT activity and delays the onset of shivering.
levels.phd:
**UCP1 mechanism.** UCP1 belongs to the SLC25 mitochondrial carrier family. Fedorenko, Lishko and Kirichok's 2012 patch-clamp studies of brown fat mitoplasts showed that UCP1 carries an H+ current that depends on long-chain fatty acids. They proposed a fatty-acid shuttling model: the fatty-acid anion is bound but cannot dissociate, and protons travel with it, so UCP1 acts as an LCFA anion/H+ symporter. This competes with the older flip-flop model, in which UCP1 exports fatty-acid anions and protonated fatty acids diffuse back across the membrane. Cryo-EM structures (2021-2023) show nucleotides binding the central cavity and locking the carrier, consistent with purine nucleotide inhibition. Fatty acids released by ATGL/HSL lipolysis overcome this block.

**Discovery in adults.** Brown fat was long thought to regress after infancy. In 2009 three NEJM papers (Cypess; van Marken Lichtenbelt; Virtanen) used 18F-FDG PET/CT to confirm metabolically active, UCP1-positive supraclavicular and paravertebral BAT in adults. BAT activity was inversely related to BMI and age and was higher in winter. FDG measures glucose uptake, but BAT burns mainly intracellular triglyceride, so FDG uptake can underestimate or mislabel thermogenic activity.

**Quantitative contribution.** Indirect calorimetry studies of mild cold (Ouellet et al., 2012) showed shivering is recruited alongside BAT. BAT oxidative metabolism accounted for only a small share of the rise in whole-body energy expenditure. Skeletal muscle is the dominant thermogenic organ in cold-exposed adults.

**UCP1-independent thermogenesis.** UCP1-knockout mice survive gradual cold acclimation, revealing other heat sources:
- **Futile creatine cycling** (Kazak et al., 2015), with creatine kinase B as a key enzyme
- **SERCA2b-mediated Ca2+ cycling** in beige fat
- In muscle, **sarcolipin** uncouples SERCA1 ATP hydrolysis from Ca2+ transport

**Developmental lineage.** Classic BAT arises from Myf5+/Pax7+ dermomyotome precursors shared with muscle. **PRDM16** determines the brown fate. Beige cells come mostly from separate precursors or from white adipocytes switching phenotype. Whether adult human supraclavicular BAT is classic or beige remains debated; transcript profiles suggest a mixture.
levels.expert:
**Clinical relevance of shivering.** Shivering raises oxygen consumption and CO2 production a great deal. In patients with limited cardiopulmonary reserve, this can cause demand ischaemia, hypoxaemia and acidosis. In neurocritical care, deliberate fever control or **targeted temperature management** after cardiac arrest or brain injury often triggers vigorous shivering. Shivering opposes cooling, raises intracranial pressure and lowers brain tissue oxygen. Bedside tools such as the **Bedside Shivering Assessment Scale (BSAS)** guide a stepwise response: surface counter-warming of the skin to reduce the cold signal, then drug options such as magnesium, buspirone, dexmedetomidine, meperidine and opioids. Neuromuscular blockade is a last resort because it hides seizures and the neurological exam. Meperidine is notably anti-shivering, partly through κ-opioid and α2-adrenergic effects. Postanaesthetic shivering arises from anaesthetic-induced redistribution and impaired thermoregulation.

**Pharmacology of BAT.** The β3 agonist **mirabegron**, approved for overactive bladder, acutely raises human BAT FDG uptake and energy expenditure. At higher exposures it also stimulates β1 receptors, raising heart rate and blood pressure. Chronic studies (O'Mara et al., 2020) showed increased BAT activity alongside better insulin sensitivity and HDL. Weight loss is small because of compensatory intake. Thyroid hormone, capsinoids (TRPV1) and bile acids (TGR5) can also activate BAT. **Imaging pitfall:** BAT FDG uptake can mimic lymphoma or metastases on oncologic PET. Warming patients before scans or giving propranolol reduces it.

**Toxicology.** **2,4-dinitrophenol** is a chemical protonophore that uncouples all mitochondria without regulation. It causes fatal hyperthermia, showing why UCP1's tight control matters. Malignant hyperthermia, by contrast, is a ryanodine receptor disorder of muscle Ca2+ handling, not an excess of BAT activity.

**Acclimatization phenotypes.** Repeated cold exposure in humans can shift heat production from shivering towards non-shivering thermogenesis (van der Lans, 2013). Real-world groups vary: Inuit populations show elevated basal metabolism, partly linked to thyroid function. Indigenous Australians studied by Scholander showed insulative hypothermic tolerance rather than extra heat production.

**Open questions:** how much humans can recruit beige fat, the true UCP1 transport mechanism, how central circuits coordinate shivering and BAT, and whether BAT activity protects against cardiometabolic disease in a causal way. A large retrospective PET cohort (Becher et al., 2021) linked BAT with lower rates of these diseases, but such data cannot prove causation.

keyPoints: The preoptic hypothalamus triggers cold thermogenesis via the raphe pallidus
Shivering turns muscle ATP use into heat, up to about 4-5x resting rate
Brown fat uses UCP1 to leak protons, releasing energy as heat instead of ATP
Norepinephrine, β-adrenergic signalling and lipolysis-derived fatty acids activate UCP1
Adults keep active supraclavicular brown fat (2009 PET studies), but muscle dominates heat production
UCP1-independent routes include futile creatine and calcium cycling

test.q: Which brain region acts as the main thermostat that triggers cold thermogenesis?
test.explain: Preoptic neurons of the hypothalamus integrate temperature signals and drive heat production. The motor cortex controls voluntary movement, and shivering is involuntary.

test.q: What does UCP1 do in brown fat mitochondria?
test.explain: UCP1 dissipates the proton gradient, so the energy from substrate oxidation is released as heat instead of being used to make ATP.

test.q: Why does brown fat look brown?
test.explain: The many iron-containing mitochondria give BAT its colour. A single large lipid droplet is the feature of white fat.

test.q: Which hormone-receptor signal mainly activates brown fat?
test.explain: Sympathetic norepinephrine acts on β-adrenergic receptors (β3, and possibly β2 in humans), raising cAMP and driving lipolysis.

test.q: Why do newborns depend heavily on brown fat?
test.explain: Infants cannot shiver effectively, so non-shivering thermogenesis from BAT between the shoulder blades is vital.

test.q: Beige (brite) adipocytes are best described as:
choices: White fat cells that store extra lipid
test.explain: Beige cells appear in white fat after cold or β-adrenergic stimulation and express UCP1. This process is called browning.

test.q: During shivering, little net movement occurs because:
test.explain: Shivering is asynchronous co-contraction of opposing skeletal muscles, so the energy becomes heat rather than motion.

test.q: Which enzyme in BAT converts T4 to active T3 locally?
test.explain: DIO2 makes local T3, which boosts UCP1 expression and works together with sympathetic input.

test.q: In cold-exposed adults, which tissue makes the largest share of extra heat?
test.explain: Calorimetry studies show BAT contributes modestly. Skeletal muscle shivering dominates thermogenesis in adults.

test.q: Heat production by the body in response to cold is called ___.
test.explain: Thermogenesis includes both shivering and non-shivering forms.

test.q: What abbreviation is used for brown adipose tissue?
test.explain: BAT stands for brown adipose tissue.

test.q: Imaging studies in 2009 found adult brown fat mainly in the ___ region, above the collarbones.
test.explain: FDG PET/CT showed active BAT in the supraclavicular and paravertebral regions.

kidTest.q: Why do we shiver when cold?
kidTest.explain: Muscles burn fuel when they move, and that makes heat.

kidTest.q: What is special about brown fat?
kidTest.explain: Brown fat works like a tiny heater.

kidTest.q: Who has lots of brown fat?
kidTest.explain: Babies can't shiver well, so brown fat keeps them warm.

kidTest.q: About what temperature does your body like to stay?
kidTest.explain: Your body keeps itself close to 37 degrees Celsius.

kidTest.q: When you are cold, your muscles shake. This is called s _ _ _ _ _ _ _ _.
kidTest.explain: Shivering makes heat.

advancedTest.q: UCP1-knockout mice survive gradual cold acclimation. This best supports:
choices: Alternative routes such as futile creatine and Ca2+ cycling
UCP1 being irrelevant to heat production in brown fat
Thyroid hormone being dispensable for heat
advancedTest.explain: Survival without UCP1 revealed UCP1-independent thermogenic cycles. It does not show that UCP1 is unimportant in normal animals.

advancedTest.q: Why might FDG PET misjudge brown fat thermogenic activity?
choices: FDG binds UCP1 and blocks its action
BAT burns mainly its own stored triglyceride
advancedTest.explain: FDG tracks glucose uptake, but BAT oxidizes mostly intracellular fatty acids, so glucose uptake and heat output can come apart.

advancedTest.q: Why is 2,4-dinitrophenol lethal while UCP1 activity is safe?
choices: DNP uncouples mitochondria with no control
DNP activates ryanodine receptors in muscle
UCP1 makes more ATP than DNP does
advancedTest.explain: UCP1 is restricted to thermogenic fat and held in check by nucleotide inhibition. DNP is an unregulated protonophore throughout the body, which causes runaway hyperthermia.

advancedTest.q: During targeted temperature management, why is surface counter-warming used against shivering?
choices: It activates brown fat to replace shivering
It raises core temperature to normal
It directly blocks the neuromuscular junction
It lowers the skin cold signal driving the hypothalamus
advancedTest.explain: Cutaneous cold input strongly drives the thermoregulatory response. Warming the skin reduces that input while the core stays cool.

lessons.title: Cold-Induced Vasoconstriction and the Hunting Reaction

levels.kid:
When you go out in the snow, your body wants to keep its warm heat inside. Your blood carries that heat around, like warm water in pipes.

So your body squeezes the little blood pipes in your skin, fingers and toes. Less warm blood goes out to the cold edges, and more stays deep inside to keep your heart and brain cozy. That is why your fingers turn pale and feel numb.

But fingers need some warmth too! So every few minutes, your body opens the pipes for a little while. A puff of warm blood rushes in, and your fingers turn pink and tingly. Then the pipes squeeze shut again. Scientists call this on-and-off pattern the **hunting reaction**, because the body seems to be hunting for the right temperature.
levels.hs:
Your body loses most of its heat through the skin, and blood flow controls how much heat reaches the skin. In the cold, your body reduces that flow. This is called **cold-induced vasoconstriction**: the small blood vessels in the skin narrow.

How it works:
- Cold sensors in the skin send signals to the **hypothalamus**, the brain's thermostat.
- The hypothalamus activates the **sympathetic nervous system**, which releases **norepinephrine** onto the smooth muscle around skin blood vessels, making them contract.
- Cold also acts directly on the vessels, making them more sensitive to this signal.

The result is that the skin acts like an insulating layer around a warm **core** (heart, brain, organs). Skin blood flow in the fingers can drop by more than 90%.

There is a cost: cold, bloodless fingers lose feeling and dexterity and risk injury. So hands, feet, ears and nose show the **hunting reaction**, also called **cold-induced vasodilation (CIVD)**. About 5 to 10 minutes after a hand is put in very cold water, the vessels suddenly open. Skin temperature rises by a few degrees, then falls again, cycling up and down.

Example: fishermen in Norway and Inuit hunters, who often work with bare hands in the cold, tend to show stronger, earlier CIVD than people who rarely face cold. This helps keep their fingers working.
levels.college:
In the cold, the body defends core temperature mainly by cutting **convective heat transfer** from core to skin. Skin blood flow is the main controlled variable, and the fingers, toes, ears and nose are the most important sites.

**Mechanisms of cold-induced vasoconstriction**
- **Reflex (neural)**: skin cold receptors, mostly TRPM8-expressing fibres, signal through the spinal cord to the preoptic area of the hypothalamus. Sympathetic noradrenergic nerves to the skin then release **norepinephrine**, which acts on **α1- and α2-adrenoceptors** on vascular smooth muscle. Cotransmitters, especially **neuropeptide Y** acting on Y1 receptors, add to the constriction.
- **Local (direct) cooling**: cooling the vessel wall moves **α2C-adrenoceptors** from inside the smooth muscle cell to its surface, so the vessel responds more to the same amount of norepinephrine. It also reduces nitric oxide signalling.

**Arteriovenous anastomoses (AVAs)** are thick-walled shunts in glabrous (hairless) skin of the palms, soles, lips, nose and ears. They are densely innervated by sympathetic nerves and close almost completely in the cold. They are the main route by which acral blood flow, and therefore heat loss, swings so widely.

**Countercurrent heat exchange** adds to the effect. In the cold, venous return shifts from superficial veins to the **venae comitantes** running beside the arteries, so outgoing arterial blood warms the returning venous blood. Heat is recycled to the core.

**Hunting reaction (CIVD)**: first described by **Thomas Lewis in 1930**, who saw finger temperature in ice water oscillate. Typically, after 5-10 min of cold, finger skin temperature rises a few °C, then falls, in repeating waves. CIVD:
- protects the skin from local cold injury and preserves manual dexterity;
- varies a lot between people, and is often weaker in people who are colder overall;
- is suppressed when the core is cooling, because protecting the core takes priority.

The trade-off is clear: constriction protects core temperature, while CIVD protects the tissue at the edges.
levels.phd:
Cutaneous vasoconstriction lowers whole-body thermal conductance. Combined with tissue insulation, it can drop finger blood flow from well over 100 mL·min⁻¹·100 mL⁻¹ in heat to near zero in the cold. Control is split between reflex and local components, each with a distinct molecular basis.

**Reflex arm.** Studies using bretylium (which blocks transmitter release) and specific antagonists, notably by Kellogg, Johnson and colleagues, showed that reflex cold vasoconstriction is roughly 60% noradrenergic (α1/α2) and about 30-40% due to the cotransmitter **NPY** acting on Y1 receptors. Remarkably, there is no active vasodilator nerve system in acral skin. Its flow is governed almost entirely by changes in constrictor tone, unlike hairy skin.

**Local arm.** Flavahan and colleagues showed that cooling generates mitochondrial **reactive oxygen species**. These activate **RhoA/Rho kinase (ROCK)**, which drives translocation of α2C-adrenoceptors from the Golgi to the plasma membrane and raises myofilament calcium sensitivity. Local cooling also inhibits NO synthase. In human microdialysis studies, Rho-kinase inhibition with fasudil blunts the local response. This pathway has been implicated in **Raynaud's phenomenon**, an exaggerated cold-induced vasospasm.

**CIVD mechanism, still debated.** There are three main hypotheses:
- Lewis's **axon reflex** model, with release of vasodilator neuropeptides (CGRP, substance P) from sensory nerves.
- **Cold paralysis** of the smooth muscle, or failure of neuromuscular transmission, once the tissue drops below about 10-12 °C, which lets the AVAs open passively.
- **Central withdrawal** of sympathetic tone.

The finding that CIVD persists after nerve block argues for a local mechanism. On the other hand, its strong suppression by whole-body cooling and its enhancement by a warm core, shown by Daanen and others, show central modulation. A plausible synthesis is that CIVD is a local release of the vessel from constriction, gated by central sympathetic drive.

**Adaptation.** Population and longitudinal studies give mixed results. Habituated groups (Inuit, Lapps, Gaspé fishermen) show strong CIVD, but repeated exposure in the laboratory often fails to raise CIVD and can even blunt it. This suggests genetic and anthropometric factors, or habituation of central drive, matter more than peripheral training. Daanen's meta-analytic work also notes large intra-individual variability, so a single test is unreliable.
levels.expert:
For clinicians and expedition physicians, the practical question is how vascular control in the hands and feet predicts and modifies cold injury risk. The injuries themselves are covered elsewhere in this unit.

**CIVD as a risk marker.** In Dutch and military studies, people with weak CIVD responses (lower mean finger temperature and slower onset in a standard immersion test) had higher subsequent rates of local cold injury. Ethnicity also matters: soldiers of African descent show weaker CIVD and higher frostbite incidence in British Army data. The predictive value for an individual is modest, though, because test-retest reliability is poor. Results also depend on water temperature, the immersed area, and the subject's core and mean skin temperature at the time.

**Modifiers clinicians can act on**
- **Keep the core warm.** A warm core is the best way to restore hand perfusion. Insulating the torso helps the fingers more than an extra glove, because it lowers central sympathetic drive.
- **Hypoxia** at altitude blunts CIVD and deepens constriction, which compounds frostbite risk in mountaineers.
- **Dehydration, exhaustion and hypoglycaemia** reduce heat production and worsen peripheral vasoconstriction.
- **Nicotine** acts as a sympathomimetic vasoconstrictor. Non-selective β-blockers can leave α-mediated vasoconstriction unopposed and worsen cold extremities, and ergot derivatives and some sympathomimetic drugs also constrict vessels.

**Raynaud's phenomenon** is the clinical extreme of local cold sensitivity. Primary Raynaud's reflects enhanced α2C/Rho-kinase signalling, and estrogen upregulates α2C expression, which helps explain the female predominance. Secondary Raynaud's, for example with systemic sclerosis, adds structural microvascular disease and has a risk of digital ulcers. Dihydropyridine calcium channel blockers are first-line drug therapy. PDE5 inhibitors and prostacyclin analogues are used for severe disease, and botulinum toxin injections, which reduce sympathetic vasoconstriction locally, are an emerging option.

**Open questions**
- What is the definitive mechanism of CIVD? Laser-Doppler and thermal imaging now resolve AVA opening events in detail.
- Can AVA physiology be exploited therapeutically? Palm cooling and warming devices use AVAs to move heat quickly.
- Can targeted pre-expedition testing or acclimatisation meaningfully reduce cold injury risk?

**Pitfall:** pale, cold fingers in a person whose core is cooling are an appropriate defence of the core, not a local problem. Warming only the hands treats the wrong target.

keyPoints: Skin vasoconstriction in the cold reduces heat loss from core to skin
Sympathetic norepinephrine (α-receptors) plus NPY drive reflex constriction
Local cooling moves α2C-receptors to the cell surface via Rho kinase
Arteriovenous anastomoses in hands, feet, ears and nose control acral blood flow
The hunting reaction (CIVD) is a cyclic vessel opening that protects fingers
A cooling core suppresses CIVD; a warm core restores hand blood flow

test.q: What is the main purpose of cold-induced vasoconstriction in the skin?
choices: To reduce heat transfer from core to skin
To raise blood glucose for fuel
To increase shivering in large muscles
test.explain: Narrowing skin vessels cuts convective heat delivery to the surface, conserving core heat. Shivering and brown fat produce heat rather than conserve it.

test.q: Which neurotransmitter do sympathetic nerves mainly release onto skin vessels in the cold?
test.explain: Sympathetic noradrenergic nerves release norepinephrine, which acts on α-adrenoceptors to contract vascular smooth muscle.

test.q: Which cotransmitter adds to reflex cold vasoconstriction?
test.explain: NPY acting on Y1 receptors contributes a substantial share of reflex vasoconstriction. Nitric oxide and bradykinin are vasodilators.

test.q: Local cooling makes skin vessels more sensitive to norepinephrine mainly by:
choices: Moving α2C-receptors to the cell surface
test.explain: Cooling triggers Rho kinase-driven translocation of α2C-adrenoceptors to the membrane, and it reduces rather than increases NO signalling.

test.q: Arteriovenous anastomoses are found mainly in:
choices: Hairless skin of hands and feet
test.explain: AVAs sit in glabrous skin of palms, soles, lips, nose and ears, where they shunt large volumes of blood.

test.q: How does countercurrent heat exchange conserve heat in a cold limb?
choices: Muscles shiver to warm blood in deep veins
Sweat glands release warmed fluid to the skin
Arterial blood warms nearby returning venous blood
Venous blood is routed to superficial skin veins
test.explain: Deep veins beside arteries pick up heat from outgoing arterial blood, returning it to the core. Superficial venous routing would lose heat.

test.q: What happens to finger temperature during the hunting reaction?
choices: It cycles up and down repeatedly
It rises once and stays high
It falls steadily to water temperature
test.explain: CIVD produces repeated waves of vessel opening and closing, so finger temperature oscillates.

test.q: Who first described the hunting reaction in 1930?
test.explain: Thomas Lewis observed oscillating finger temperatures in ice water and named the hunting reaction.

test.q: What effect does a cooling body core have on the hunting reaction?
choices: It speeds up the first wave
It has little or no effect
test.explain: Defending the core takes priority, so whole-body cooling suppresses CIVD, while a warm core enhances it.

test.q: The hunting reaction is also called cold-induced ___ (CIVD).
test.explain: CIVD stands for cold-induced vasodilation, the periodic opening of vessels in cold extremities.

test.q: Which brain region acts as the body's thermostat in triggering cold vasoconstriction?
test.explain: Cold signals reach the preoptic hypothalamus, which drives sympathetic output to skin vessels.

test.q: Fishermen who often work bare-handed in cold water tend to show a ___ hunting reaction than people rarely exposed to cold.
test.explain: Cold-habituated groups such as Norwegian fishermen and Inuit hunters tend to show stronger, earlier CIVD.

kidTest.q: What does your body do to the blood pipes in your skin when it is cold?
kidTest.explain: Squeezing the pipes keeps warm blood deep inside your body.

kidTest.q: Why do your fingers turn pale in the cold?
kidTest.explain: With less blood flowing in, fingers look pale and feel numb.

kidTest.q: Which body parts does the body most want to keep warm?
kidTest.explain: The body keeps warm blood around the heart and brain first.

kidTest.q: During the hunting reaction, your fingers sometimes turn pink. Why?
kidTest.explain: The pipes open for a moment and let warm blood in.

kidTest.q: The on-and-off pattern in cold fingers is called the h _ _ _ _ _ _ reaction.
kidTest.explain: It's called the hunting reaction because the body seems to hunt for the right temperature.

advancedTest.q: CIVD persists after local nerve block but is suppressed by whole-body cooling. The best interpretation is:
choices: CIVD is caused by rising core temperature alone
CIVD is a local event modulated by central sympathetic drive
CIVD depends on shivering heat reaching the fingers
CIVD is purely a central reflex with no local part
advancedTest.explain: Persistence after nerve block shows a local mechanism, while suppression by core cooling shows central gating. Together they support a local release gated by sympathetic tone.

advancedTest.q: Why might a non-selective β-blocker worsen cold extremities?
choices: It raises nitric oxide in acral skin
It blocks α1-receptors on skin arterioles
It increases brown fat heat production
advancedTest.explain: Blocking β2-mediated dilation leaves α-adrenergic vasoconstriction unopposed, so cold-induced narrowing deepens.

advancedTest.q: A climber at altitude has cold, white fingers. Which action best restores hand perfusion?
choices: Applying heat packs to the hands alone
Insulating the torso and warming the core
advancedTest.explain: A warm core lowers central sympathetic drive and permits CIVD. Warming just the hands treats the wrong target, and nicotine constricts vessels.

advancedTest.q: Laboratory cold training often fails to raise CIVD, though habituated populations show strong CIVD. This suggests:
choices: Genetic, body-build or central factors matter more
CIVD testing in laboratories is too unreliable to use
Habituated groups have more shivering capacity
Peripheral vessel training is the main driver
advancedTest.explain: Since repeated lab exposure doesn't reliably enhance CIVD, population differences likely reflect genetics, anthropometry or central habituation rather than local training.

lessons.title: The Cold Shock Response and Cold Water Immersion

levels.kid:
Have you ever jumped into a very cold pool and gasped? That gasp is called the **cold shock response**. Your skin has tiny cold sensors. When icy water hits them, they shout an alarm to your brain all at once.

Your body reacts before you can think. You take a giant breath, then breathe very fast. Your heart races. If your face is under the water when you gasp, you could breathe in water. That is why cold water is dangerous even for good swimmers.

The good news: the big gasp calms down in about one minute. Experts teach a simple rule: if you fall into cold water, float on your back and stay still. Wait for your breathing to calm, then make a plan.
levels.hs:
Most people imagine cold water kills by **hypothermia**, a dangerous drop in core body temperature. In fact, many cold water deaths happen in the first few minutes, long before the core cools. The main culprit is the **cold shock response**.

When water below about 15 °C suddenly covers the skin, cold receptors fire intensely. This triggers:
- **The gasp reflex**: one large, uncontrollable breath.
- **Hyperventilation**: rapid breathing that you can barely control.
- **A surge in heart rate and blood pressure**, driven by the sympathetic nervous system (the "fight or flight" system) and by blood vessels in the skin clamping shut.

If the head is underwater during the gasp, water is inhaled, which can cause drowning. Breath-holding time can drop to just a few seconds.

The response peaks within the first 30 seconds and fades over about 1 to 3 minutes. Water safety educators teach the **1-10-1 rule**: about 1 minute to control your breathing, about 10 minutes of useful muscle movement before your arms and hands weaken, and roughly 1 hour before hypothermia makes you lose consciousness.

A real example: many drownings in cold lakes in spring involve strong swimmers close to shore. The advice "**float first**" (lie back, keep the airway clear, let the gasp pass) saves lives.
levels.college:
Cold water immersion is usually described in four stages, each with its own main threat:
- **Cold shock** (0 to 3 min): respiratory and cardiovascular reflexes.
- **Swim failure** (about 3 to 30 min): the arms and legs cool and stop working.
- **Hypothermia** (more than 30 min): the core temperature falls.
- **Circum-rescue collapse**: sudden deterioration just before, during or after rescue.

**Mechanism of cold shock.** Cold receptors in the skin are mainly TRPM8-expressing fibres. They respond to the *rate* of skin cooling, not only its level. Sudden immersion produces a massive afferent burst. This drives:
- An inspiratory **gasp** and **hyperventilation**. Breathing can rise several-fold, which washes out CO2 and causes **hypocapnia**. Low CO2 narrows brain arteries, which can cause dizziness and confusion.
- Sharply reduced **breath-hold time**, which raises the risk of breathing in water.
- A sympathetic surge with tachycardia, raised cardiac output and peripheral vasoconstriction. Blood pressure rises steeply and the heart has to work much harder.

The response scales with water temperature. It begins below roughly 25 °C, is strongest around 10 to 15 °C, and changes little below that. Wetsuits and drysuits reduce it, mainly by slowing how fast the skin cools.

**Swim failure** happens because cooled muscles and nerves conduct and contract more slowly, and movement becomes clumsy. This is a local effect in the arms and legs and is not caused by low core temperature. Swimming also strips away the warm water layer next to the skin. In cold water, swimming speeds heat loss compared with staying still.

**Habituation**: as few as about 5 brief cold immersions can reduce the cold shock response by roughly half, and the effect can last for months. This is a central nervous system adaptation in how the brain responds to the cold signal. It is a different process from acclimatisation of heat production.
levels.phd:
Much of the quantitative work on cold shock comes from Tipton, Golden and colleagues at Portsmouth. Head-out immersion in 10 °C water typically raises minute ventilation several-fold within seconds. The gasp can reach volumes of 1 to 2 L or more, and breath-hold time falls from a typical value of around 45 to 60 s in air to well under 10 s. Respiratory frequency and heart rate peak in the first 30 s and decline over about 3 min. Ventilation is driven by the cutaneous signal and is out of step with metabolic demand, producing hypocapnic alkalosis. A fall in cerebral blood flow velocity, measured by transcranial Doppler in the middle cerebral artery, has been reported.

**Afferent coding.** The cold shock response follows the dynamic (rate-of-change) component of cold receptor firing. This explains why rapid, total-body immersion is more provoking than slow cooling. Cold receptors on the face and chest appear to contribute more than those on the limbs.

**Autonomic conflict.** Shattock and Tipton (2012) proposed that some sudden immersion deaths reflect **autonomic conflict**. The cold shock response activates the sympathetic system. Facial immersion together with breath-holding triggers the **diving response**, a vagal reflex that slows the heart, acting through trigeminal input. When both are active at once, the heart receives opposing signals. Studies of immersion with the face submerged and the breath held show a high incidence of arrhythmias, mostly supraventricular and junctional rhythms and ectopic beats, often appearing on the breakpoint of the breath-hold. In a heart that is already vulnerable, for example with long QT syndrome (especially LQT1), ischaemia or cardiomyopathy, this conflict may trigger a fatal arrhythmia.

**Habituation** reduces the ventilatory and heart-rate components substantially. It is specific to the stimulus: it reflects a central change in how the brain responds to the same skin cooling, rather than general stress tolerance. It can be weakened by anxiety and by hypoxia, which is relevant to how people train for open water.

**Circum-rescue collapse** has been attributed to loss of hydrostatic pressure support when a casualty is lifted vertically out of the water. Blood pools in the legs, less blood returns to the heart, and blood pressure can fall sharply in a body already compromised by cold. A drop in stress hormones once rescue seems near may also contribute.
levels.expert:
**Clinical and operational implications.**
- **Epidemiology.** Analyses of immersion deaths suggest that a large share of fatalities happen early, in the cold shock and swim failure stages, rather than from true hypothermia. This shaped modern guidance. Lifejacket use and **"Float to Live"** (the RNLI campaign) target the first minutes, rather than relying on insulation alone.
- **Rescue technique.** Lift casualties **horizontally** where possible, and handle them gently to reduce the risk of circum-rescue collapse. Pre-rescue collapse is described as well, possibly from dehydration caused by cold diuresis together with reduced vigilance.
- **Cardiac screening.** In unexplained sudden death in water, especially in young people, molecular autopsy for channelopathies, mainly KCNQ1 variants (LQT1) and RYR2 variants (CPVT), is recommended. Relatives should be offered cascade screening. Clinicians should advise patients with known channelopathies, cardiomyopathy or coronary disease about the danger of sudden immersion and breath-hold diving.

**Pitfalls.**
- Assuming a strong swimmer can reach shore. Swim performance in cold water bears little relation to performance in a pool.
- Treating every immersion death as hypothermia. Core temperature at recovery may be close to normal.
- Recommending HELP (Heat Escape Lessening Posture) or huddling before the cold shock response has settled. Breathing control comes first.

**Cold water swimming and "cold therapy."** Winter swimming and ice baths are popular, and claims of benefit for mood, inflammation and metabolism are widespread. Reviews find that the evidence is mostly small, uncontrolled or confounded studies. Real risks include arrhythmias, cold shock drowning, and immersion pulmonary oedema in swimmers. For athletes, regular cold water immersion after resistance training can blunt muscle hypertrophy and strength gains, an effect shown in studies such as Roberts et al. (2015). This makes timing matter.

**Open questions.**
- How individual risk is distributed between ventilatory hyperreactivity and arrhythmic susceptibility, and whether either can be predicted.
- How long habituation lasts and the best way to build it in military and offshore training.
- Whether cold shock contributes to deaths labelled as hypothermia or drowning in cold seawater, and how often.
- The role of trigeminal and other receptor subtypes in initiating autonomic conflict.

keyPoints: Sudden cold water immersion triggers a gasp, hyperventilation and a heart rate and blood pressure surge
Many cold water deaths happen in the first minutes, before hypothermia develops
Immersion stages: cold shock, swim failure, hypothermia, circum-rescue collapse
The 1-10-1 rule: 1 min breathing, 10 min useful movement, about 1 h to hypothermic unconsciousness
Autonomic conflict between cold shock and the diving response can trigger arrhythmias
About five short immersions can roughly halve cold shock by habituation

lessons.title: Accidental Hypothermia: Stages, Arrhythmias and Afterdrop

levels.kid:
Your body works best when its inside temperature is about 37 degrees Celsius. When someone gets very cold for a long time, that inside temperature can drop. This is called **hypothermia**.

At first, the person shivers hard. That is the body's way of making heat, like rubbing your hands together. If they get colder, they stop shivering. They get sleepy and confused, and their heart beats slowly.

A very cold heart is like a clock that is easy to knock out of rhythm. So rescuers move cold people gently and keep them lying down.

Doctors have a saying: "Nobody is dead until they are warm and dead." Some very cold people who seemed lifeless have been warmed up and lived!
levels.hs:
**Accidental hypothermia** means the body's core temperature has fallen below 35 °C without anyone causing it on purpose. Normal core temperature is about 37 °C. Common causes are cold water, mountain accidents, and old or ill people in cold homes.

Doctors sort hypothermia into **stages** by core temperature:
- **Mild (32-35 °C):** strong shivering, fast breathing, clumsiness, poor judgment.
- **Moderate (28-32 °C):** shivering fades, confusion and drowsiness, slow heart rate.
- **Severe (below 28 °C):** unconsciousness, very slow or absent breathing and pulse, high risk of cardiac arrest.

Cold slows the heart's electrical system. A cold heart is "irritable": rough handling can trigger **ventricular fibrillation (VF)**, a chaotic quivering in which the heart pumps no blood.

**Afterdrop** is when core temperature keeps falling even after the person is rescued. Part of the reason is that colder blood from the arms and legs returns to the core.

A real example: in 1999, Swedish doctor Anna Bågenholm fell through ice while skiing in Norway. Her core temperature reached 13.7 °C. She was rewarmed with a heart-lung bypass machine and recovered. That case is why doctors say people may survive severe hypothermia even when they look dead.
levels.college:
Hypothermia develops when heat loss (conduction, convection, radiation, evaporation) exceeds heat production. Water conducts heat about 25 times faster than air, which makes immersion especially dangerous. Risk rises with alcohol, sedatives, hypothyroidism, hypoglycemia, trauma, and extremes of age.

**Staging.** The classic thresholds are mild (32-35 °C), moderate (28-32 °C) and severe (<28 °C). Some systems add profound hypothermia below about 24 °C. In the field, where thermometers are unreliable, the **Swiss staging** system uses clinical signs: conscious and shivering, impaired consciousness without shivering, unconscious, and no vital signs. Revisions now favor estimating cardiac arrest risk from consciousness level.

**Physiology by stage.**
- Mild: catecholamine surge, shivering, tachycardia, vasoconstriction, **cold diuresis** (shifting of blood to the core raises central volume, so the kidneys excrete more water).
- Moderate: shivering stops as fuel and neural drive fail. Metabolic rate falls about 6-7% per °C. Paradoxical undressing may occur.
- Severe: coma, fixed pupils, apnea, hypotension.

**Cardiac effects.** Cooling slows depolarization and repolarization:
- Sinus bradycardia, then atrial fibrillation, which is common below about 32 °C.
- Prolonged PR, QRS and QT intervals.
- The **Osborn (J) wave**, a positive hump at the junction of the QRS complex and the ST segment.
- Below about 28 °C, the VF threshold drops. Below about 24 °C, asystole becomes likely.

**Afterdrop** is the continued fall in core temperature after removal from the cold. It has two components: ongoing conductive heat flow down the temperature gradient from the core into the cooler outer tissues, and convective return of cold peripheral blood.

**Rescue collapse** is cardiac arrest during extraction or rewarming. It is linked to afterdrop, hypovolemia when the person is lifted upright, and mechanical irritation of the cold heart. That is why rescuers handle victims horizontally and gently.
levels.phd:
**Electrophysiology of the cold heart.** Temperature affects ion channel gating with a Q10 of about 2-3. Cooling slows the sodium current (I_Na) upstroke, so conduction velocity falls and QRS widens. It also slows the potassium currents I_Kr and I_Ks, so action potential duration and the QT interval lengthen.

The **Osborn wave** reflects a transmural voltage gradient during early repolarization. Epicardial cells carry more transient outward current (I_to) than endocardial cells, and hypothermia accentuates the epicardial spike-and-dome. This was shown in canine wedge preparations by Yan and Antzelevitch. J-wave amplitude correlates roughly inversely with temperature.

Arrhythmogenesis depends on several factors acting together. Dispersion of repolarization, slowed conduction and calcium overload all lower the VF threshold. Calcium overload comes from Na+/K+-ATPase inhibition and altered sarcoplasmic reticulum handling. Acidosis and potassium shifts add to the instability.

**Afterdrop mechanisms: the controversy.** Afterdrop was long attributed to cold peripheral blood returning convectively when vasoconstriction relaxed. Webb (1986) and later Giesbrecht's human immersion studies argued that much of it is conductive. Heat keeps flowing from the core down a steep gradient into cold peripheral tissue, independent of blood flow. Supporting this, afterdrop occurs even in models with no circulation.

In practice both mechanisms operate, and their relative contributions depend on the rewarming method. Active rewarming of the extremities, especially hot-water immersion, causes vasodilation and can deepen afterdrop or cause hypotension. That is the basis for warming the trunk first. In Giesbrecht's studies, afterdrop was modest in shivering subjects, roughly 0.5-1 °C.

**Cold-induced neuroprotection.** Cerebral metabolic rate falls roughly 6-7% per °C. At about 18 °C, the brain can tolerate circulatory arrest for far longer than at normothermia. This principle is exploited in deep hypothermic circulatory arrest for aortic arch and neurovascular surgery. It explains why survival with good neurological outcome is possible when cooling preceded asphyxia or arrest. Arrest that came first and cooling that came later carries a far worse prognosis.

Cold also causes coagulopathy, which standard laboratory assays performed at 37 °C miss. Other effects include left-shifted oxyhemoglobin dissociation, impaired drug metabolism, and hyperglycemia from insulin suppression.
levels.expert:
**Prognostication and resource triage.** For hypothermic cardiac arrest, the most important decision is whether to go to **extracorporeal life support (ECLS)**. This means VA-ECMO or cardiopulmonary bypass, which rewarm while also supporting the circulation.

The **HOPE score** (Pasquier et al., 2018) predicts survival from age, sex, mechanism (asphyxia or not), CPR duration, serum potassium and temperature. It outperforms potassium cutoffs alone. A HOPE score of 10% or more supports ECLS. Serum potassium above roughly 12 mmol/L suggests cell death and an asphyxial mechanism, such as an avalanche victim buried without an air pocket.

The ERC and Wilderness Medical Society guidelines recommend transporting arrested patients directly to an ECLS-capable center. Mechanical CPR devices make long transports feasible.

**Resuscitation nuances.**
- Check for a pulse for up to 60 seconds, because profound bradycardia with vasoconstriction can mimic arrest.
- Defibrillation is often ineffective below about 30 °C. Guidelines suggest up to three shocks, then deferring further attempts until the patient has rewarmed.
- Vasoactive drugs are typically withheld below about 30 °C and given at longer intervals until normothermia, because cold slows drug clearance and causes accumulation.
- **Intermittent CPR** (Gordon et al., 2015) is acceptable when continuous CPR is impossible during extrication, for example in the mountains. Below 28 °C, short pauses are tolerated.

**Pitfalls.**
- Low-reading thermometers and tympanic probes in a cold ear canal underestimate core temperature. Use esophageal probes in intubated patients.
- Blood gases and clotting tests are run at 37 °C, so they mask cold-induced coagulopathy.
- Missed causes: hypoglycemia, intoxication, sepsis, myxedema, and trauma hidden by numbness.
- Rewarming shock and electrolyte shifts can occur once the patient warms.

**Open questions.** Optimal rewarming rate after ECLS is uncertain. So is the role of post-rewarming targeted temperature management and the neurological outcome predictors after prolonged low-flow periods. Some data show survival of about 50% or more with ECLS in non-asphyxial cases.

For a neurosurgery-minded learner, the same cold that kills on a mountain protects in the operating room. Deep hypothermic circulatory arrest uses controlled cooling to protect the brain during aneurysm surgery, and accidental hypothermia teaches its limits.

keyPoints: Hypothermia: core temperature below 35 °C; staged mild, moderate and severe
Shivering stops in moderate hypothermia as consciousness falls
Cold slows conduction: bradycardia, AF, long QT, Osborn J waves
Below about 28 °C the VF threshold drops; handle patients gently and horizontally
Afterdrop is the continued core cooling after rescue, from conductive and convective mechanisms
Hypothermic arrest can be survivable with ECLS; the HOPE score guides triage

advancedTest.explain: Peripheral vasodilation returns cold blood to the core and drops blood pressure, so the trunk is warmed first.

lessons.title: Frostbite and Non-Freezing Cold Injury

levels.kid:
When it is very cold, your body protects its middle, where your heart and brain live. To do that, it sends less warm blood to your fingers, toes, nose and ears. If they get cold enough for long enough, they can actually freeze. That is called **frostbite**.

Frozen skin turns pale, hard and numb. Tiny ice crystals form, like frost on a window, and they can hurt the cells.

There is another cold injury where nothing freezes. If feet stay cold and wet for days, like in soggy boots, they can get hurt too. This is called **trench foot**.

The best plan is to stay dry, wear warm gloves and socks, and warm up gently. Never rub frozen skin.
levels.hs:
**Frostbite** is a freezing injury to tissue. It happens when skin and the tissue under it cool below roughly -0.5 to -2 degrees Celsius, so ice forms. The usual targets are fingers, toes, nose, ears and cheeks. These parts are far from the body's core, they have a lot of surface area, and blood flow to them is cut back in the cold.

Doctors describe frostbite by depth:
- **Frostnip**: cold, pale, numb skin with no ice inside the tissue. It recovers fully after warming.
- **Superficial frostbite**: the skin freezes and clear blisters form after rewarming.
- **Deep frostbite**: deeper tissues freeze, blood-filled blisters appear, and tissue may die. Dead tissue turns black and hard, a change called **gangrene**.

**Non-freezing cold injury (NFCI)** damages tissue without freezing it. The classic form is **trench foot** (also called immersion foot). It comes from hours to days of cold, wet conditions, often between 0 and 15 degrees Celsius. It was common among soldiers in World War I trenches. The feet first look white and numb, then turn red, swollen and painful once rewarmed. Pain and sensitivity to cold can last for years.

The main treatment for frostbite is **rapid rewarming** in warm water. One key rule: don't thaw a frozen part if it might refreeze. A freeze-thaw-refreeze cycle causes far more damage than staying frozen a little longer.
levels.college:
Cold injuries fall into two groups: **freezing** (frostbite) and **non-freezing** (NFCI). Risk factors are shared: cold, wind, wetness, tight boots, dehydration, immobility, previous cold injury, smoking, and low body temperature. Some groups also face higher risk, including people of African descent, as reported in military data.

**Mechanisms of frostbite injury**
- **Direct cellular injury**: Ice first forms *outside* cells. This makes the fluid around cells more concentrated, so water is pulled out of them and they shrink and dehydrate. Very fast freezing can also form ice *inside* cells, which kills them directly.
- **Progressive microvascular injury**: After thawing, the damaged endothelium (the lining of blood vessels) sets off inflammation. Mediators such as prostaglandin F2-alpha and thromboxane A2 cause vessels to tighten, platelets to clump, and clots to form in small vessels. This **reperfusion injury** is often the bigger cause of tissue death.

**Classification** uses either degrees (first to fourth, similar to burns) or a simpler split into superficial versus deep. Bone scans can grade frostbite after rewarming (the Cauchy classification).

**Field and hospital care**
- Treat hypothermia first. Remove wet clothing.
- Rewarm rapidly in a whirlpool at about 37 to 39 degrees Celsius until the part is red and soft. This is very painful, so strong pain relief is needed.
- Leave blood-filled blisters intact. Clear blisters may be drained. Aloe vera is used for its anti-thromboxane effect, and ibuprofen for its anti-prostaglandin effect.

**NFCI** follows a set course: during cold exposure, intense vasoconstriction makes the foot white and numb; next comes a reddish-blue stage of poor circulation; then **hyperemia**, a burning, swollen, painful foot that lasts weeks; and finally a post-hyperemic stage with lasting pain, cold sensitivity and sweating problems. The injury is thought to involve both nerves and blood vessels. Large myelinated nerve fibres are especially vulnerable.
levels.phd:
Frostbite injury happens in phases that overlap: pre-freeze, freeze-thaw, vascular stasis, and late ischemia. As tissue cools, its blood flow falls through sympathetic vasoconstriction. Cold-induced vasodilation can briefly bring blood back, but this protective response weakens during prolonged exposure or hypothermia. Ice usually forms in the extracellular space first, because those fluids nucleate at higher temperatures. This **solute effect** concentrates salts outside cells. The concentrated fluid draws water out, cells shrink, membranes are damaged, and proteins denature. Faster cooling, as in high wind chill or contact with metal or volatile fuels, favours intracellular ice, which is nearly always lethal to the cell. This physics is the same reasoning cryobiologists use to optimise cooling rates.

The freeze is not the whole story. Rabbit-ear models from the 1970s and 1980s (Robson, Heggers and colleagues) showed that blister fluid is rich in PGF2-alpha and thromboxane B2, the stable metabolite of TXA2. Blocking these eicosanoids improved tissue survival. This work was the basis for the Heggers/McCauley protocol, which combines topical aloe vera and systemic ibuprofen. After reperfusion, neutrophils accumulate and reactive oxygen species form, as in other ischemia-reperfusion injuries. Microthrombi then progressively block capillaries, and tissue that looked viable at thaw goes on to necrose. This progression is why thrombolysis can work.

Refreezing is especially destructive. Thawing releases inflammatory mediators and causes oedema, and ice that re-forms in this primed tissue enlarges the injury. Experimental data show that a freeze-thaw-refreeze cycle produces more tissue loss than prolonged freezing alone.

NFCI is less well understood. Proposed mechanisms include:
- Prolonged vasoconstriction causing ischaemic neuropathy, with large myelinated fibres especially vulnerable.
- Endothelial dysfunction, with impaired nitric oxide-mediated vasodilation.
- Reperfusion injury during the hyperaemic phase.

Irwin's and Ungley's work on wartime cohorts (Ungley described immersion foot in shipwreck survivors in World War II) set out the clinical staging. Whether NFCI is mainly a neuropathy or mainly a vasculopathy remains debated. Thermography studies show lasting abnormal vasospastic responses to cold stress. These responses resemble secondary Raynaud's phenomenon and suggest damage to the sympathetic control of skin blood vessels.
levels.expert:
Modern frostbite care targets the thrombotic phase. In a landmark 2007 trial, Bruen and colleagues showed that **tissue plasminogen activator (tPA)**, given within 24 hours of rewarming and guided by angiography, cut digital amputations from about 41% to 10% in severe frostbite. The best results come early; benefit falls off sharply after 24 hours of warm ischaemia. Diagnostic algorithms favour **technetium-99m bone scintigraphy** (triple-phase scanning or SPECT/CT) to assess perfusion and predict where amputation will be needed. The aim is to identify salvageable tissue early, because clinical appearance in the first days is notoriously misleading.

**Iloprost**, a prostacyclin analogue that dilates vessels and inhibits platelets, was tested by Cauchy and colleagues in a 2011 randomised trial in Chamonix. Amputations were 0% with iloprost alone versus 60% with buflomedil in grade 3-4 frostbite. Iloprost won FDA approval for frostbite in 2024. It suits remote or expedition settings and patients with contraindications to thrombolysis, such as recent trauma. Adjuncts such as sympathectomy, hyperbaric oxygen and pentoxifylline have weaker evidence.

Surgical lesson: "frostbite in January, amputate in July." Demarcation can take 1 to 3 months. Early debridement is reserved for infection, wet gangrene or compartment syndrome. Imaging now permits earlier, more confident decisions.

Pitfalls:
- Thawing in the field when refreezing is possible.
- Rubbing with snow, or using dry heat, which burns numb skin.
- Missing coexisting hypothermia.
- Using tPA with head injury or other bleeding risks; in neurosurgical polytrauma this is a real conflict.

NFCI is a major military occupational problem, with UK Ministry of Defence data showing a disproportionate burden. Diagnosis is clinical, often supported by cold-sensitivity testing with thermography. Chronic NFCI pain behaves as **neuropathic pain**, so treatment uses neuropathic agents such as amitriptyline or gabapentinoids rather than standard analgesics. Prevention is mostly logistical: drying and changing socks, foot inspections, and limiting how long feet stay wet.

Open questions:
- Biomarkers that predict tissue viability.
- The best time windows for thrombolytics.
- Whether NFCI represents a small-fibre neuropathy.
- Individual susceptibility, including genetic or ethnic differences in cold-induced vasodilation.

keyPoints: Frostbite is tissue freezing; NFCI (trench foot) damages tissue without ice
Extracellular ice dehydrates cells; fast cooling causes lethal intracellular ice
Reperfusion, eicosanoids (PGF2a, TXA2) and microthrombi drive much of the tissue loss
Rewarm rapidly in warm water, but avoid thawing if refreezing is possible
tPA and iloprost reduce amputations in severe frostbite when given early
NFCI causes long-lasting neuropathic pain and cold sensitivity

test.q: What distinguishes frostbite from trench foot?
choices: Trench foot is caused by a bacterial infection
Trench foot occurs in dry and windy weather
Frostbite involves ice forming in the tissue
Frostbite affects the hands, trench foot the face
test.explain: Frostbite is a freezing injury. Trench foot is a non-freezing injury caused by prolonged cold, wet exposure.

test.q: Which condition recovers fully after warming, with no ice in the tissue?
test.explain: Frostnip is superficial cooling without tissue freezing, so it fully recovers. Trench foot can cause pain that lasts for years.

test.q: Why is extracellular ice damaging to cells?
choices: It blocks oxygen from entering the lungs
It pulls water out, dehydrating the cells
It warms the cells through friction
It makes cells swell and burst from water
test.explain: Extracellular ice concentrates solutes outside cells, so water leaves them and they shrink. Swelling and bursting is the reverse of what happens.

test.q: What is the recommended way to rewarm a frostbitten hand?
choices: Rubbing the hand with clean snow
Slowly warming it over several days
Holding it near an open campfire
test.explain: Rapid rewarming in warm water is standard. Rubbing and dry heat damage numb tissue.

test.q: Why should a frozen toe not be thawed if it may refreeze?
choices: Thawed tissue loses its sense of touch
Refreezing primes far worse tissue damage
The toe will return to normal on its own
test.explain: A freeze-thaw-refreeze cycle causes more tissue loss than staying frozen longer.

test.q: Which mediators are found in high levels in frostbite blister fluid?
test.explain: These eicosanoids cause vasoconstriction and platelet clumping. This is why ibuprofen and aloe vera are used.

test.q: What appearance do blood-filled blisters usually indicate?
test.explain: Blood-filled blisters suggest deeper injury. Clear blisters are typical of superficial frostbite.

test.q: What is the burning, red, swollen stage of NFCI called?
test.explain: After the cold, white phase, the rewarmed foot becomes hyperemic: red, swollen and painful for weeks.

test.q: In classic experimental studies of cold nerve injury (e.g. Denny-Brown), which nerve elements proved most vulnerable?
test.explain: Classic experimental work on prolonged cold ischaemia found large myelinated fibres most susceptible to damage. More recent NFCI research also highlights small-fibre (C-fibre) involvement, which underlies the chronic pain and cold sensitivity.

test.q: Dead, black, hard tissue after deep frostbite is called ___.
test.explain: Gangrene is tissue death and may require amputation.

test.q: What is the World War I name for non-freezing cold injury of the feet?
test.explain: Soldiers in wet trenches developed this injury, also called immersion foot.

test.q: Which painkiller is used in frostbite partly for its anti-thromboxane effect?
test.explain: Ibuprofen blocks eicosanoid production, limiting vasoconstriction and clotting.

kidTest.q: Which body parts get frostbite most easily?
kidTest.explain: Fingers and toes are far from the warm middle of the body and get less warm blood in the cold.

kidTest.q: What forms inside skin that has frostbite?
kidTest.explain: Tiny ice crystals form and can hurt the cells.

kidTest.q: What causes trench foot?
choices: Eating lots of cold ice cream
kidTest.explain: Trench foot comes from feet staying cold and wet for a long time, such as in soggy boots.

kidTest.q: What should you NOT do to frozen skin?
kidTest.explain: Rubbing frozen skin hurts it more.

kidTest.q: Freezing of fingers or toes is called f _ _ _ _ _ _ _ _.
kidTest.explain: Frostbite means the skin has frozen.

advancedTest.q: A digit looks viable at thaw but becomes necrotic days later. Which mechanism best explains this?
choices: Progressive microthrombosis and reperfusion injury after thaw
Delayed loss of the shivering response in the affected limb
Continued growth of intracellular ice once the digit is warm
Bacterial toxins released from the skin's surface flora
advancedTest.explain: Endothelial injury, eicosanoids and microthrombi progressively block capillaries after reperfusion. Ice cannot keep forming in warm tissue.

advancedTest.q: Why do contact with metal and high wind chill produce worse cellular injury?
choices: Slower cooling allows more solute buildup in cells
Metal and wind make the extracellular fluid less salty
Rapid cooling triggers protective vasodilation in the skin
Faster cooling favours intracellular ice formation
advancedTest.explain: Rapid cooling outpaces water leaving cells, so ice forms inside them, which is nearly always lethal.

advancedTest.q: A climber with deep frostbite also has a recent head injury. Which therapy fits best?
choices: Early surgical amputation before demarcation occurs
Dry-heat rewarming to limit the risk of brain swelling
Iloprost, avoiding the bleeding risk of thrombolysis
Thrombolysis with tPA, given urgently within 24 hours
advancedTest.explain: tPA carries a bleeding risk that is unacceptable with head trauma. Iloprost dilates vessels and inhibits platelets with less bleeding risk.

advancedTest.q: Persistent cold-induced vasospasm on thermography after NFCI suggests:
choices: Lasting damage to sympathetic control of skin vessels
Excess brown fat thermogenesis occurring in the affected limb
Full recovery of the normal cold-induced vasodilation
Ongoing ice crystal formation within the deeper soft tissues
advancedTest.explain: Abnormal responses that resemble secondary Raynaud's phenomenon point to neurovascular damage, which fits the neuropathy-versus-vasculopathy debate about NFCI.
